sourcing: This practice set follows the public description of the IELTS Academic Reading paper: three passages with different question types (here matching information to paragraphs, multiple choice, and Yes / No / Not given) and one Writing Task 1 about a chart. It is shorter than the real papers: the real Academic Reading paper has 3 passages, 40 questions and 60 minutes, while this set has 3 passages and 30 questions. The real Writing paper has two tasks (Task 1: at least 150 words, about 20 minutes; Task 2: an essay of at least 250 words, about 40 minutes; 60 minutes in total). This set has Task 1 only; for Task 2, practise an essay on a topic of your own choice in 40 minutes. All passages and questions were written by EnglishAcademy, and the chart data is invented. It is not official IELTS material. Official practice material is free on ielts.org.
scoringNote: IELTS has no pass mark. Each skill is reported as a band score from 0 to 9, and each university or employer sets the bands it asks for. The rating below is therefore NOT an IELTS band score. It is only rough feedback on this practice set. Your institution tells you what you need for your course.

aufgabe1.title: Matching information
aufgabe1.instruction: The passage below has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? Choose the correct letter, A–H. You may use any letter more than once.

anzeigen.title: A · Early parks
anzeigen.body: Many public parks in Europe began as private gardens or hunting grounds that their owners opened to the public. In the nineteenth century, fast-growing industrial cities built new parks for a different reason. Reformers argued that fresh air and open space would improve the health of workers who lived in crowded, smoky streets.

anzeigen.title: B · Health
anzeigen.body: Studies in several countries link living near green space with lower levels of stress. Researchers add a warning, however. People who choose to live near a park may differ from other people in income and lifestyle, so the link alone does not show that parks cause better health.

anzeigen.title: C · Heat
anzeigen.body: Trees give shade, and they release water vapour that cools the air around them. On a hot day, a street lined with trees can be several degrees cooler than a street of bare paving. Planners now treat trees as a way of reducing heat, not only as decoration.

anzeigen.title: D · Rainwater
anzeigen.body: Soil and plants absorb rain, but concrete does not. In a city with many paved surfaces, heavy rain runs quickly into the drains, and flooding becomes more likely. Gardens that collect rain and let it sink slowly into the ground can reduce this risk.

anzeigen.title: E · Wildlife
anzeigen.body: Even small green spaces can support insects, birds and other animals, especially when they contain a mixture of native plants. Closely mown lawns, by contrast, support few species. A growing number of councils therefore leave strips of grass uncut until late in the summer.

anzeigen.title: F · Cost
anzeigen.body: Building and looking after green space costs money, and public budgets are under pressure. Some councils ask volunteers to help with planting, while others charge for events held in parks. Critics fear that the quality of a park will then depend on how wealthy the local area is.

anzeigen.title: G · Fairness
anzeigen.body: Within a single city, access to green space is often uneven. Wealthier districts tend to have more parks, and larger ones, than poorer districts. Researchers describe this as a question of fairness and not simply of taste.

anzeigen.title: H · Small spaces
anzeigen.body: Not every city has room for a large park. Planners are therefore turning to roofs, walls and the small, often unused spaces between buildings. These “pocket parks” may be only a few metres across, but they are often very busy.

items.situation: an explanation of why industrial cities built public parks in the nineteenth century
a warning that a link between green space and lower stress may not show cause and effect
a statement that planting trees can make hot streets cooler
a description of how green space can help to prevent flooding
a way of managing grass that helps wildlife
a mention of people who give their time to help plant
a statement that some districts of a city have fewer parks than others
a mention of planting on roofs and walls
a statement that very small parks can be popular
a statement that public money for parks is limited

aufgabe2.title: Multiple choice
aufgabe2.instruction: Read the passage and choose the correct answer to each question: a, b, c or d.

text.label: Passage 2 — Magazine article
text.title: Keeping Time: How the Railways Changed the Clock
text.body:
Until the early nineteenth century, almost nobody in Britain needed to know the exact time. Each town set its clocks by the sun, with noon being the moment when the sun stood highest. Because the sun reaches its highest point later in the west, noon in Bristol came about ten minutes after noon in London. For people travelling on foot or on horseback, a difference of that size was invisible.

The railways changed this. A train that left London at a fixed hour could reach a station far away within a few hours, and a timetable printed in London time made little sense to a passenger who looked up at the station clock and saw a different time. Early timetables sometimes listed several local times side by side, which confused travellers and left the companies open to complaints. In 1840 one company in the west of England began to run all of its trains by London time. Others followed gradually, and by 1847 most railway companies had adopted what became known as “railway time”.

Many towns did not welcome the change. A few put two minute hands on their public clocks, one showing local time and one showing railway time, so that people could use whichever they preferred. The objections were not only practical. Some people felt that a distant company had no right to decide what time it was in their own town, and for them the question was one of principle as well as convenience.

The telegraph made a common time much easier to keep. From the 1850s, time signals could be sent along telegraph wires from an observatory at Greenwich to stations all over the country, so that clocks could be checked every day. Even so, the law was slow to catch up. It was not until 1880 that Parliament made Greenwich time the legal time throughout Great Britain. By then, the new habit was so widespread that the law changed little in everyday life.

Historians still disagree about how quickly small towns and villages changed their clocks, because the records are patchy. What is clear is the pattern. A new technology created a problem that nobody had had before, ordinary people and businesses solved it in practice, and only afterwards did the law confirm what had already happened.

items.prompt: Why was noon in Bristol later than noon in London?
options: Bristol clocks were less accurate.
The sun reaches its highest point later in the west.
Bristol followed the railway timetables.
Church bells in Bristol rang later.
items.answer: The sun reaches its highest point later in the west.

items.prompt: Why did a difference of ten minutes between towns matter little before the railways?
options: Most towns used the same clocks.
Clocks were checked every day.
Few people travelled fast enough to notice it.
Noon was not important to anyone.
items.answer: Few people travelled fast enough to notice it.

items.prompt: What problem did early railway timetables cause?
options: Trains left earlier than the printed times.
The times in the timetable did not match the station clock.
There were not enough printed copies for passengers.
Timetables were only printed for the west of England.
items.answer: The times in the timetable did not match the station clock.

items.prompt: What happened in 1840?
options: Parliament made London time the legal time.
Most railway companies adopted London time.
One company began to run its trains by London time.
Telegraph wires reached every station.
items.answer: One company began to run its trains by London time.

items.prompt: Why does the writer mention clocks with two minute hands?
options: To show that some towns used both local time and railway time.
To show that railway time was always accurate.
To explain how the telegraph worked.
To show that railway companies built the clocks.
items.answer: To show that some towns used both local time and railway time.

items.prompt: According to the writer, some people objected to railway time because
options: it made their journeys longer.
it was less accurate than the sun.
they felt a distant company should not decide their time.
they could not read the new timetables.
items.answer: they felt a distant company should not decide their time.

items.prompt: How did the telegraph help?
options: It made trains travel faster.
It let stations receive the time from Greenwich.
It replaced timetables.
It made local clocks unnecessary in 1850.
items.answer: It let stations receive the time from Greenwich.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about the law of 1880?
options: It caused a large change in everyday life.
It forced railway companies to change their timetables.
It ended the use of local time in villages at once.
It made official a habit that was already common.
items.answer: It made official a habit that was already common.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about historians?
options: They agree that small towns changed quickly.
They disagree about how fast small places changed, because records are incomplete.
They think railway time was a mistake.
They have found no records at all.
items.answer: They disagree about how fast small places changed, because records are incomplete.

items.prompt: What is the writer’s main point?
options: The railways were more important than the telegraph.
Local time was better than a common time.
A new technology can change people’s habits before the law does.
Parliament should have acted sooner.
items.answer: A new technology can change people’s habits before the law does.

aufgabe3.title: Yes / No / Not given
aufgabe3.instruction: Read the passage. Do the statements agree with the claims of the writer? Choose “Yes” if the statement agrees with the writer, “No” if it contradicts the writer, and “Not given” if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks. Careful: “No” means the text says something different, not that the text says nothing.

text.label: Passage 3 — Science magazine
text.title: What Happens When We Sleep?
text.body:
For a long time, sleep was treated as a passive state, a kind of switching off of the brain. Recordings of brain activity, made from the 1950s onwards, overturned that view. During the night the brain moves through a repeating pattern of stages. Each cycle lasts roughly ninety minutes, and some stages are almost as active as waking life.

The best-known stage is rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most vivid dreaming takes place. For years it was assumed that dreaming was the main purpose of REM sleep. That assumption now looks too narrow. Researchers increasingly link both REM and deep sleep to memory: new experiences seem to be replayed and sorted, with some stored and others discarded. How this happens in detail is still disputed, and anyone who claims to know the full answer is going beyond the evidence.

The body clock also changes with age. During adolescence it moves later, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until late in the evening, yet most schools start early in the morning. A small number of schools have tried later start times. The early reports are encouraging, but they come mostly from short trials. It would be premature to conclude that a later start raises exam results, and I would not yet recommend that every school change its timetable.

Caffeine works by blocking the chemical signals that make us feel tired. In a typical adult, about half of it is still active in the body after five hours. A coffee drunk at four in the afternoon can therefore affect sleep at bedtime, even in people who feel no effect at all. Because they do not feel anything, they rarely connect a poor night with the coffee.

People are also poor judges of their own sleep. Many of us sleep for longer than we believe, particularly after a restless night. This does not mean that tiredness is imaginary, but it does suggest that worrying about sleep can make it feel worse than it was.

Finally, there is the popular claim that every adult needs eight hours of sleep. The figure is a useful average, but needs differ from person to person. A healthy adult who wakes refreshed after seven hours has little reason to worry, and little reason to force a longer night.

items.prompt: Researchers once believed that the sleeping brain was inactive.
A sleep cycle lasts about ninety minutes.
The writer believes that dreaming is the main purpose of REM sleep.
Deep sleep lasts longer in the first half of the night than in the second half.
Teenagers usually feel sleepy earlier in the evening than adults do.
Some schools have tried starting lessons later.
The writer is sure that later school start times raise exam results.
Afternoon coffee can disturb sleep even when the drinker feels nothing.
Sleep-tracking apps give an accurate picture of a night’s sleep.
The writer believes that every adult needs eight hours of sleep.

schreiben.instruction: Academic Writing Task 1. Summarise the information in the chart by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words. In the real test you have about 20 minutes for this task.

grafik.caption: How adults in the imaginary town of Fairhaven travelled to work (invented data by EnglishAcademy, not real statistics)

aufgabe: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features of the chart.
Make comparisons where relevant. Do not give your own opinion and do not explain the reasons: Task 1 describes only what the chart shows.
Write at least 150 words. (In the real Writing paper, Task 2 follows: an essay of at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. This set does not include it; practise it with an essay topic of your own.)
aufbau: Introduction: paraphrase the title of the chart in one sentence (what, who, where, when).
Overview: two or three sentences with the main trends, without detailed figures: which category is the largest, and which changed most?
Body paragraph 1: the largest category and the one that fell, with figures from the chart.
Body paragraph 2: the categories that rose, with figures from the chart.
No conclusion with an opinion is needed. Do not repeat the overview.
redemittel: Overall, the most common way of getting to work was … throughout the period.
The proportion of adults who … rose from 6 per cent in 2000 to 14 per cent in 2020.
… fell steadily / increased sharply / remained almost unchanged.
The most striking change was the rise in …
By contrast, … / Whereas … / In comparison with …
checklist: The introduction says what the chart shows, for whom and for which years.
There is an overview with the main trends, and it has no detailed figures.
At least four figures are quoted and read correctly from the chart.
A change over time is described, not just single values.
The text compares categories (for example car and bicycle) and does not list every number.
There is no personal opinion and no invented reason.
The text has at least 150 words and uses linking words (whereas, however, by contrast).
